new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand: Charpentier's blanket remark for the interior (central) languages of South Malakula, applied by Lynch & Crowley to the Lendamboi/Letemboi varieties: strong primary stress on the penultimate syllable, with the following final vowel reduced almost to inaudibility (hence subscript vowels in the transcriptions).
new_statements.exceptions: None; L&C caution that the phonemic status of the reduced final vowels is unclear.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level remark on citation forms in wordlists; it is a generalisation over 'the languages of the center of the island', not a statement made for Letemboi alone, and it is reported through Lynch & Crowley rather than read in Charpentier's atlas.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog lete1241 'Letemboi-Repanbitip' (ISO nms) is the language Lynch & Crowley 2001 call Lendamboi (Letemboi/Lendamboi is a village name used as the list label in Tryon 1976); it comprises four mutually intelligible interior varieties, Ayiauleian, Mbotkot, Natanggan (moribund) and Nioleien, the last being Tryon's 'Repanbitip(mbangir)'. The stress remark is Charpentier's generalisation over the interior ('center of the island') languages of South Malakula, applied by Lynch & Crowley to the Lendamboi transcriptions, not a statement made for Letemboi alone.

sources.note: Survey, not a description. Footnote 6 on p. 71, attached to Charpentier's transcriptions of the four Lendamboi varieties (Ayiauleian, Mbotkot, Natanggan, Nioleien = Tryon's Repanbitip), reports Charpentier (1982a:63): in the languages of the centre of the island there is a strong tonic accent on the next-to-last syllable and the final vowel is so destressed as to be almost unrecognizable; L&C add that the phonemic status of the reduced vowels is unclear. States that the only sources are Charpentier's and Tryon's wordlists plus unverified Deacon 1934 snippets.
